## Report: Does Boiled Garlic Water Cure COVID-19?

**Conclusion: This claim is false.** There is no scientific evidence that boiled garlic water — or garlic in any form — cures, treats, or prevents COVID-19.

**What the evidence shows:**

The World Health Organization directly addressed this claim in its official COVID-19 "Mythbusters" list, stating: "Garlic is a healthy food that may have some antimicrobial properties. However, there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). This is echoed by health ministries and hospitals worldwide (https://health.gov.tt/covid-19-faqs-and-mythbusters/covid-19-mythbusters).

Independent fact-checking organizations have repeatedly investigated and debunked viral claims about garlic (often combined with onion, ginger, or lemon) curing or destroying COVID-19. AFP Fact Check consulted health professionals as early as February 2020 who confirmed "there is no evidence for its use as an effective treatment" (https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19). Rappler's fact-checkers similarly rated claims that heat, garlic, and ginger prevent COVID-19 as FALSE, noting "there is no official cure or preventive treatment for COVID-19" (https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/264621-heat-garlic-ginger-cure-covid-19/).

**Important nuance:** Garlic does contain compounds with some general antimicrobial properties, which is why the myth persists — but "some antimicrobial activity in a lab setting" is entirely different from "curing an active viral infection in humans." No clinical trials have demonstrated garlic water is effective against SARS-CoV-2.

**Bottom line:** This belief is a well-documented health myth. COVID-19 requires evidence-based prevention (vaccination) and treatment (antivirals, supportive care as advised by physicians) — not home remedies like garlic water, which pose no proven benefit and could give false confidence that delays proper care.
